events.title: Siege of Calagurris
events.summary: Sertorius relieved Calagurris in 74 against Pompey and Metellus; after his death the town held out against Pompey's legate Lucius Afranius until 72, its starving defenders reduced to eating their women and children. 'Calagurritan hunger' became proverbial.

battle.significance: Last major resistance of the Sertorian war.

events.title: Pompey's repulse at Pallantia
events.summary: Pompey besieged the Vaccaean stronghold of Pallantia and had undermined its timber walls when Sertorius arrived; Pompey burned his works and retreated to join Metellus. It was one of several Sertorian successes in 74 that kept the war going despite his dwindling base.

battle.significance: Checked Pompey's advance into the Meseta.

events.title: Lex Terentia Cassia frumentaria
events.summary: The consuls Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus and Gaius Cassius Longinus restored subsidised grain distributions, abolished by Sulla, at five modii a month for some 40,000 citizens, financed by compulsory purchases of Sicilian grain. Verres was among the governors who administered the purchases.

events.title: Licinius Macer's campaign for the tribunate
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Licinius Macer, also a historian of early Rome, agitated for the restoration of the tribunes' powers removed by Sulla, urging the plebs to refuse military service. Sallust gives him a fiery speech. He was convicted of extortion in 66, with Cicero presiding, and killed himself.

events.title: Spartacus defeats the praetor Varinius
events.summary: After escaping the blockade of Vesuvius, Spartacus defeated the praetor Publius Varinius and his legates Furius and Cossinius in a series of engagements in Campania and Lucania, capturing Varinius' lictors and horse. His army swelled with herdsmen and runaways to tens of thousands.

sides.strength: several thousand rising to tens of thousands

battle.significance: Turned the breakout into a full-scale slave war.

events.title: Lucullus destroys the retreating Pontic army on the Aesepus and Granicus
events.summary: Starved out at Cyzicus, Mithridates' army retreated west; Lucullus caught one column in snow at the Rhyndacus and another at the crossing of the Aesepus and Granicus, killing or capturing tens of thousands. The king escaped by sea and lost much of his fleet in a storm.

events.title: Spartacus defeats Cassius Longinus at Mutina
events.summary: Marching north toward the Alps after beating both consuls, Spartacus routed the proconsul of Cisalpine Gaul, Gaius Cassius Longinus, near Mutina. Instead of crossing the Alps he turned back south, for reasons the sources do not agree on.

battle.significance: Left the road out of Italy open.

events.debate: Why Spartacus turned back (overconfidence, his followers' wish to plunder Italy, or fear of the Alpine crossing) is unknowable.

events.title: Pompey defeats and executes Perperna
events.summary: Perperna, who had murdered Sertorius and taken command, was drawn into an ambush and routed by Pompey. Captured hiding in a thicket, he offered Sertorius' correspondence with leading senators; Pompey burned the letters unread and had him executed.

events.title: Cotta's siege and sack of Heraclea Pontica
events.summary: Marcus Aurelius Cotta besieged Heraclea, which had admitted a Pontic garrison, for two years; it fell by betrayal in 70 and was plundered and burned, Cotta taking the statue of Heracles from the agora. The Senate later restored the Heracleots' freedom and Cotta was expelled from the Senate for embezzlement.

sides.strength: Cotta's army and fleet of Triarius

battle.significance: Memnon's local history gives an unusual civic view of the war.

events.title: Lucullus takes Amisus
events.summary: After a siege of nearly two years, Lucullus stormed Amisus, whose Pontic commander Callimachus fired the city as he fled; Lucullus tried in vain to save it, wept at the destruction, and then rebuilt it and restored its freedom. Among the captives was the grammarian Tyrannion, later Cicero's librarian.

battle.significance: Completed the conquest of coastal Pontus.

events.title: Appius Claudius demands Mithridates from Tigranes
events.summary: Lucullus sent his brother-in-law Appius Claudius Pulcher to Antioch to demand that Tigranes II surrender his father-in-law Mithridates. Appius addressed the 'King of Kings' simply as king, won over several of his vassals, and was refused, making war with Armenia inevitable.

events.title: Crassus destroys the Gallic and German breakaway force
events.summary: After breaking through Crassus' line in Bruttium, Spartacus' army split again; a group of Gauls and Germans under Castus and Gannicus encamped by a Lucanian lake near Mount Cantenna was attacked by Crassus, who killed 12,300 of them, all, Plutarch says, with their wounds in front.

battle.significance: Preceded the final battle on the Silarus.

events.title: Crassus walls off the toe of Italy
events.summary: When Spartacus, cheated by Cilician pirates who had promised to ferry him to Sicily, was trapped in Bruttium, Crassus dug a ditch and wall some 300 stadia (c. 55 km) long across the isthmus. Spartacus broke through on a snowy night by filling a section of the ditch with earth, timber and corpses.
events.debate: The line's location (Catanzaro isthmus or further north, near the Sila) is uncertain.

events.title: Pompey's trophy on the Pyrenees
events.summary: On his return from Spain Pompey set up a monumental trophy on the summit of the Pyrenean pass at Panissars, recording that he had brought 876 towns from the Alps to the borders of Further Spain under Roman control. Its foundations were identified in 1984 at Col de Panissars.

events.title: Census of 70: 910,000 citizens
events.summary: The censors Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus and Lucius Gellius Poplicola, the first since 86, registered 910,000 citizens, roughly double the previous count, as the enfranchised Italians were at last enrolled. They also expelled 64 senators, including Gaius Antonius Hybrida and Publius Lentulus Sura.
events.detail: The figure marks the real completion of the Social War settlement. It also shows how the electorate now far exceeded those who could ever vote in person at Rome, a structural fact that shaped late Republican politics: elections were decided by those who could be brought to the Campus Martius, and candidates canvassed the Italian municipia.

events.title: Lex Plautia recalls the Lepidans
events.summary: A tribune Plautius carried a law recalling those who had followed Lepidus and later Sertorius. Caesar, then a young senator, spoke for it because it would restore his brother-in-law Lucius Cornelius Cinna.

events.title: Birth of Virgil
events.summary: Publius Vergilius Maro was born on 15 October 70 at Andes near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul, then still without full citizenship, to a family of modest landowners. He was educated at Cremona, Milan and Rome, then with the Epicurean Siro at Naples.

events.title: Caesar's funeral speeches for Julia and Cornelia
events.summary: As quaestor Caesar delivered the funeral oration for his aunt Julia, Marius' widow, tracing her descent from King Ancus Marcius and from Venus, and displayed Marius' images in the procession for the first time since Sulla. He then praised his young wife Cornelia, an unusual honour for a young woman.

events.title: Catulus dedicates the rebuilt Capitoline temple
events.summary: Quintus Lutatius Catulus dedicated the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, rebuilt after the fire of 83 with columns Sulla had taken from the Olympieion at Athens. Catulus' name on the pediment was resented by Caesar, who tried as praetor in 62 to transfer the dedication to Pompey.

events.title: Lucullus takes Nisibis
events.summary: Turning south after the mutinous retreat from Artaxata, Lucullus stormed Nisibis in Mygdonia on a stormy night in autumn 68, capturing Tigranes' brother Gouras and the engineer Callimachus. It was his last success: the army wintered there, and Clodius stirred the troops against him.

events.title: Pirates burn the fleet at Ostia
events.summary: Pirates entered the harbour of Ostia, burned a consular fleet and kidnapped two praetors with their lictors, as well as relatives of Marcus Antonius Creticus. Grain shipments to Rome were disrupted and prices soared, preparing opinion for the lex Gabinia.

events.title: Lex Calpurnia de ambitu
events.summary: The consul Gaius Calpurnius Piso, under pressure from the tribune Gaius Cornelius, carried a law against electoral bribery that disqualified the convicted from office for life and expelled them from the Senate. Under it Publius Autronius Paetus and Publius Sulla lost the consulships they had won for 65.

events.title: Lex Cornelia binds praetors to their edicts
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Cornelius carried a law that praetors must administer justice according to the edict they published at the start of the year, ending ad hoc favours. It was a milestone in the development of the praetorian edict into a stable body of law.

events.title: Pompey and Metellus quarrel over Crete
events.summary: The Cretan cities, besieged by Quintus Caecilius Metellus, offered their surrender to Pompey, whose lex Gabinia gave him authority over all coasts. Pompey sent his legate Lucius Octavius, who fought alongside the Cretans against Metellus' troops at Lappa and Hierapytna. Metellus ignored him and completed the conquest.

events.title: Hasmonean civil war: Hyrcanus II against Aristobulus II
events.summary: On the death of Queen Salome Alexandra, her younger son Aristobulus II defeated his brother Hyrcanus II near Jericho and took the kingship and high priesthood. The Idumaean Antipater persuaded Hyrcanus to flee to the Nabataean king Aretas III, who besieged Aristobulus in the Temple at Jerusalem.
events.detail: This quarrel brought Rome into Judaea: both brothers appealed to Pompey's legates, and the Sadducee-Pharisee division mapped onto the dynastic one, with the Pharisees and Antipater behind Hyrcanus. Josephus' account derives in part from Nicolaus of Damascus, Herod's court historian, and is favourable to Antipater.

events.title: Manilius' law on freedmen's votes
events.summary: Immediately on entering office on 10 December 67, the tribune Gaius Manilius carried a law distributing freedmen among all tribes; amid violence on the Capitol it was annulled by the Senate the next day. He then turned to his successful bill giving Pompey the war against Mithridates.

events.title: Pompey and Lucullus meet at Danala
events.summary: Pompey and Lucullus met at Danala in Galatia; the courtesies, with both lictors' fasces wreathed in laurel, turned to recriminations, Lucullus calling Pompey a vulture who came to feed on others' kills. Pompey annulled Lucullus' arrangements and took all but 1,600 of his soldiers.

events.title: Pompey's agreement with Phraates III
events.summary: Pompey renewed friendship with the Parthian king Phraates III, encouraging him to attack Tigranes, but later treated him with contempt, refusing him the title King of Kings and sending Afranius to occupy Gordyene, which Phraates claimed. The Euphrates boundary agreed with Sulla in 96 became ambiguous.

events.title: Mithridates escapes to Colchis and the Bosporus
events.summary: Defeated at night near Dasteira on the Lycus, Mithridates, refused asylum by Tigranes, fled through Colchis, wintered at Dioscurias, and in 65 passed along the Caucasian coast through the lands of the Heniochi and Achaei to the Cimmerian Bosporus, where his son Machares killed himself.

events.title: Pompey defeats the Iberians of the Caucasus
events.summary: Pursuing Mithridates, Pompey invaded Iberia (Kartli), defeated King Artoces on the Pelorus river after the king burned the bridge over the Cyrus, and took his children as hostages. Pompey turned back before reaching the Caspian, allegedly three days' march away, deterred by snakes and terrain.

battle.significance: Brought Roman arms to the Caucasus for the first time.

events.title: Crassus' censorship and the Egyptian plan
events.summary: Censor with Catulus, Marcus Licinius Crassus proposed to annex Egypt under Alexander's supposed will and to enrol the Transpadanes as citizens. Catulus blocked both, the censors resigned without completing the census, and Caesar, as aedile, was linked to the Egyptian scheme.

events.title: Lex Papia expels non-citizens
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Papius carried a law expelling non-citizens from Rome and setting up a court to try false claims to citizenship. In 62 the poet Archias, protégé of the Luculli, was prosecuted under it and defended by Cicero.

events.title: Scaurus lifts the siege of Jerusalem
events.summary: Pompey's quaestor Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, arriving in Syria, accepted 400 talents from Aristobulus II and ordered Aretas III to raise the siege of Jerusalem; Aristobulus defeated the retreating Nabataeans and Hyrcanus at Papyron. Both brothers then courted Pompey.

events.title: Birth of Horace
events.summary: Quintus Horatius Flaccus was born on 8 December 65 at Venusia in Apulia, son of a freedman who worked as a coactor (auction agent) and gave him a costly education at Rome and Athens.

events.title: Senate dissolves the collegia
events.summary: A senatus consultum abolished most collegia (neighbourhood and trade associations) and banned the Compitalia games, which they organised, as instruments of political violence. Clodius restored them by law in 58.

events.title: Cicero's consular campaign: the Commentariolum and In toga candida
events.summary: Cicero's canvass for 63 is documented by the Commentariolum petitionis, a handbook of electioneering addressed to him under the name of his brother Quintus, and by his speech In toga candida against his rivals Catiline and Gaius Antonius, preserved in fragments with Asconius' commentary. He topped the poll as a novus homo.
events.debate: Authenticity of the Commentariolum is disputed; many accept Quintus, others see a later rhetorical exercise. Either way it reflects real practice.

events.title: Lex Labiena restores election of priests
events.summary: The tribune Titus Labienus restored the Domitian system of electing members of the major priestly colleges by seventeen tribes chosen by lot, which Sulla had abolished. It made possible Caesar's election as pontifex maximus later that year.

events.title: Pro Murena: Cicero defends the consul-elect
events.summary: In the middle of the Catilinarian crisis Cicero, with Hortensius and Crassus, defended the consul-elect Lucius Licinius Murena against an ambitus charge brought by the defeated candidate Servius Sulpicius Rufus and Cato. Cicero teased Cato's Stoicism and Sulpicius' legal pedantry; Murena was acquitted.
events.detail: Cicero's argument was frankly political: with Catiline in arms, Rome could not afford to start 62 with only one consul. Cato, after the speech, is said to have remarked 'What a witty consul we have!' The case is a classic example of how ambitus law was enforced, and evaded.

events.title: Scaurus' expedition against the Nabataeans
events.summary: Pompey had marched toward Petra in 63 when news of Mithridates' death turned him back; his legate Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, governing Syria, invaded Nabataea and, through Antipater's mediation, accepted 300 talents from Aretas III. Scaurus celebrated it on coins as aedile in 58 showing Aretas kneeling beside a camel.

events.title: Metellus Nepos and Caesar suspended from office
events.summary: The tribune Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos, Pompey's agent, proposed recalling Pompey to restore order with his army. Cato and Quintus Minucius Thermus vetoed it and violence broke out in the Forum; the Senate suspended Nepos and the praetor Caesar, who backed him. Nepos fled to Pompey; Caesar was reinstated after dismissing his lictors.

events.title: Cicero's Pro Archia
events.summary: Cicero defended the citizenship of the Syrian Greek poet Aulus Licinius Archias, client of the Luculli, prosecuted under the lex Papia, and turned the speech into a celebration of literature and humane learning. Archias had promised an epic on Cicero's consulship.

events.title: Pompey visits Posidonius at Rhodes
events.summary: On his way home Pompey called on the Stoic philosopher-historian Posidonius at Rhodes, ordering his lictors not to knock at the door and lowering his fasces before the philosopher. Posidonius, though in pain from gout, lectured him on the theme that only the good is honourable.
events.debate: Pompey visited Posidonius in 66 and again in 62; Posidonius wrote a monograph on Pompey's campaigns.

events.title: Pompey lands at Brundisium and disbands his army
events.summary: Returning from the East with an undefeated army, Pompey landed at Brundisium in December 62 and, against widespread fear that he would repeat Sulla, dismissed his soldiers to their homes until his triumph. He then found he could not get his eastern settlement ratified or land for his veterans.
events.detail: The decision is one of the hinges of the late Republic. By acting constitutionally Pompey lost his leverage, and the obstruction of Lucullus, Cato, Metellus Celer and Crassus over the next eighteen months pushed him into the coalition with Caesar and Crassus. Plutarch also places here his divorce of Mucia, half-sister of Metellus Celer and Nepos, for adultery reportedly with Caesar.

events.title: Ariovistus defeats the Aedui at Magetobriga
events.summary: The Sequani and Arverni, rivals of the Aedui, hired the Suebic king Ariovistus with some 15,000 Germans; at Magetobriga (or Admagetobriga) he crushed the Aedui, who lost their nobility and hostages. Ariovistus then seized a third of the Sequani's land and settled 120,000 Germans in Gaul. The Aeduan druid Diviciacus went to Rome to plead for help.

battle.significance: Created the pretext for Caesar's intervention in 58.

events.debate: Date between 63 and 60; site unknown (perhaps near Pontailler or Moigte-de-Broie, both unproven).

events.title: Revolt of the Allobroges under Catugnatus
events.summary: Despite their loyalty during the Catilinarian affair, the debt-burdened Allobroges rose under Catugnatus and attacked Narbonese towns. The governor Gaius Pomptinus defeated them at Solonium in 61; he had to wait until 54 for his triumph.

events.title: Pompey buys the consulship for Afranius
events.summary: Pompey had his legate Lucius Afranius elected consul for 60 by open bribery, distributing money from his own gardens; the Senate passed decrees allowing magistrates' houses to be searched. Afranius proved, said Cicero, a consul whose only skill was dancing.

events.title: Clodius acquitted of sacrilege
events.summary: Tried before a specially constituted court for profaning the Bona Dea rites, Publius Clodius claimed to have been at Interamna that night; Cicero destroyed his alibi by testifying that Clodius had visited him in Rome. The jury acquitted 31 to 25, bought, said Cicero, with money from Crassus.
events.detail: Caesar, the injured husband and pontifex maximus, declined to testify against Clodius but divorced Pompeia because 'Caesar's wife must be above suspicion'. Cicero's evidence made Clodius his mortal enemy; Plutarch adds that Cicero's wife Terentia, jealous of Clodius' sister Clodia, pushed him to testify. Cicero's letter to Atticus describing the bribed jurors is one of the liveliest documents of Roman politics.

events.title: Caesar forgoes his triumph to stand for the consulship
events.summary: Returning from Further Spain in summer 60, Caesar asked permission to stand for the consulship in absence so that he could keep his imperium and celebrate a triumph. Cato talked the request out until sunset on the last day, and Caesar crossed the pomerium, giving up the triumph.

events.title: Defeat of the Flavian land bill
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Flavius proposed land for Pompey's veterans, to be funded from the eastern revenues; the consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer opposed it so vehemently that Flavius imprisoned him, and Celer had the wall of the prison broken to summon the Senate to his cell. Pompey dropped the bill.

events.title: Bribery on both sides in the elections for 59
events.summary: To match Caesar's alliance with the rich Lucius Lucceius, the optimates funded Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus with a common chest; even Cato, Suetonius says, admitted the bribery was in the public interest. Caesar and Bibulus were elected.

events.title: Burebista's Dacian kingdom
events.summary: The Getic-Dacian king Burebista, advised by the high priest Decaeneus, united the Dacians, destroyed the Boii and Taurisci on the middle Danube (c. 60), and sacked the Greek cities of the Black Sea from Olbia to Apollonia. Strabo credits him with 200,000 warriors; Caesar planned a war against him before his death, and Burebista was murdered about the same time.
events.detail: An inscription from Dionysopolis (Balchik) honours Akornion, a citizen who served as Burebista's envoy to Pompey in 48, showing that the king negotiated with the Pompeians on the eve of Pharsalus. After his death the kingdom split into four or five parts, which spared Rome a united Dacia until Decebalus.
events.debate: Dates of Burebista's reign (c. 82-44) and the extent of his realm are uncertain.

events.title: Frescoes of the Villa of the Mysteries
events.summary: In a suburban villa outside Pompeii's Herculaneum Gate, a room was painted in the Second Style around 60 with a continuous megalographic frieze of near life-size figures in a Dionysiac ritual: a reading boy, a flagellation, a winged figure, a bride's toilette. It is the most celebrated surviving Roman wall-painting of the Republic.
events.debate: Interpretation (Dionysiac initiation, bridal rite, or a combination) is unresolved; date 70-50.

events.title: Caesar remits a third of the Asian tax contract
events.summary: Caesar, as consul, carried a law remitting a third of the price the publicani had bid for the taxes of Asia, which Crassus and his equestrian allies had been pressing for since 61 and Cato had blocked. Caesar warned the contractors not to bid so recklessly again.

events.title: Ptolemy XII recognised as friend and ally
events.summary: A law of Caesar recognised Ptolemy XII Auletes as king and 'friend and ally of the Roman people', in return for a promised 6,000 talents to Caesar and Pompey, roughly a year's revenue of Egypt. Auletes borrowed the money from the Roman banker Gaius Rabirius Postumus.
events.detail: The payment ruined the king's finances: taxes rose, Alexandrian discontent grew, and when Rome annexed Cyprus (ruled by Auletes' brother) in 58 without his objecting, he was driven out. The debts bound Egypt to Roman creditors and to Caesar personally, the background to Caesar's demand for repayment in Alexandria in 48.

events.title: Ariovistus declared king and friend
events.summary: In Caesar's consulship the Senate gave Ariovistus, who now dominated eastern Gaul, the titles 'king and friend' of the Roman people, with gifts. A year later Caesar would cite his own generosity as proof of Ariovistus' ingratitude.

events.title: Bibulus watches the skies
events.summary: After being driven from the Forum with a basket of dung tipped over his head, his fasces broken, Caesar's colleague Marcus Bibulus withdrew to his house for the rest of 59 and announced that he was watching the heavens for omens, technically invalidating every assembly. Wags dated documents to the consulship 'of Julius and Caesar'.
events.detail: Obnuntiatio gave the optimates a legal argument that all Caesar's legislation of 59 was void, which is why Caesar so feared prosecution as a private citizen and insisted on moving directly from his Gallic command to a second consulship. Bibulus also posted edicts attacking Caesar and Pompey that crowds gathered to read.

events.title: The Vettius affair
events.summary: The informer Lucius Vettius claimed a plot by young optimates, including Curio, Brutus and Lucius Lentulus, to murder Pompey, then changed his list, adding Lucullus and Cicero's son-in-law. He was found strangled in prison. Cicero suspected Caesar had staged it.

events.title: Clodius transfers to the plebs
events.summary: To become eligible for the tribunate, the patrician Publius Clodius Pulcher had himself adopted by a plebeian, Publius Fonteius, who was younger than he; Caesar as pontifex maximus presided and Pompey took the auspices, within hours of Cicero's complaints in a speech in court. Fonteius emancipated him at once.

events.title: Publication of the acta of Senate and people
events.summary: One of Caesar's first acts as consul was to have the proceedings of the Senate and of the people published daily. The acta diurna, posted publicly and copied for readers in the provinces, continued under the Principate (without the Senate's debates, which Augustus suppressed) as a kind of official gazette.

events.title: Pompey marries Caesar's daughter Julia
events.summary: In April or May 59 Julia, aged about seventeen and already betrothed to Servilius Caepio, married Pompey, aged forty-seven; Caepio was compensated with Pompey's daughter. The marriage, by all accounts affectionate, sealed the alliance, and Caesar married Calpurnia, daughter of Lucius Calpurnius Piso, consul designate for 58.

events.title: Cicero's Pro Flacco
events.summary: Cicero defended Lucius Valerius Flaccus, his praetor of 63, on charges of extortion in Asia. The speech's attacks on Greek witnesses and on the Jews of Rome, whose gold for the Temple Flaccus had confiscated, preserve important evidence for Jewish communities in Asia and Rome. Flaccus was acquitted.

events.title: Panic at Vesontio
events.summary: At Vesontio (Besançon), where Caesar seized the Sequani's main town and supply base, tales of the Germans' size and ferocity caused panic; officers wrote their wills and soldiers threatened mutiny. Caesar shamed them by announcing he would march with the Tenth legion alone, which then became his favourite.

events.title: Clodius destroys Cicero's house and builds a shrine to Liberty
events.summary: After Cicero's flight, Clodius had his Palatine house, bought from Crassus for 3.5 million sesterces, demolished and dedicated part of the site to Libertas, with a statue said to be a Greek courtesan's from Tanagra. Cicero's villas at Tusculum and Formiae were also plundered.

events.title: Ptolemy XII expelled from Alexandria
events.summary: Driven out by Alexandrians angry at taxes and at his acquiescence in the loss of Cyprus, Ptolemy XII travelled to Rome via Rhodes, where Cato advised him to go home. In Rome he lived at Pompey's Alban villa and spent borrowed money to buy his restoration, while his daughter Berenice IV took the throne.

events.title: Senate destroys altars of Isis
events.summary: The Senate repeatedly ordered the private altars of Isis and Sarapis on the Capitol destroyed (58, 53, 50 and 48); in 50 the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus took an axe to a temple door himself when workmen refused. In 43 the triumvirs reversed policy and voted a public temple of Isis and Sarapis.

events.title: Caesar blocks the Helvetii at Geneva
events.summary: The Helvetii, having burned their twelve towns and four hundred villages, set out on 28 March 58 to cross through the Roman province at Geneva. Caesar hurried from Rome, broke the Rhône bridge, stalled their envoys, and fortified the left bank with a wall and ditch nineteen Roman miles long, forcing them to take the route through Sequanian territory.
events.detail: Caesar's own figures for the migrants, 368,000 people including 92,000 men under arms, come from 'tablets in Greek letters' found in their camp; few modern scholars accept them. Orgetorix, the noble who had planned the migration as a bid for kingship, died, probably by suicide, before it began. The Helvetian migration let Caesar intervene in Gaul with the pretext of protecting the province and Rome's allies the Aedui.
events.debate: Motives for the migration (German pressure, Orgetorix's ambition, land shortage) and its size are much debated.

events.title: Murder of the Alexandrian envoys
events.summary: An embassy of a hundred Alexandrians led by the philosopher Dio came to Rome to argue against Ptolemy XII's restoration; agents of the king killed many of them at Puteoli and Dio himself in Rome. Marcus Caelius Rufus was later prosecuted for involvement, which Cicero rebutted in Pro Caelio.

events.title: Street war of Clodius and Milo
events.summary: From late 57 the armed bands of Clodius, now aedile-designate, and of the tribune Titus Annius Milo, backed by Pompey and the optimates, fought for control of the streets. In November Clodius' men attacked Cicero's builders, set fire to Quintus Cicero's house and assaulted Cicero on the Sacred Way; Milo obstructed Clodius' election by watching for omens.
events.detail: The gang war made normal public business impossible for five years and is the backdrop to every political event until Milo killed Clodius at Bovillae in 52. Both sides used gladiators and freedmen; Clodius' strength lay in the neighbourhood collegia and the grain distribution system, Milo's in money and gladiatorial troupes. Modern work (Lintott, Tatum, Vanderbroeck) stresses that the gangs were political instruments, not mere crime.

events.title: Belgic siege of Bibrax
events.summary: The combined Belgic army attacked Bibrax, a town of the Remi, with the Gallic siege method of surrounding the walls and showering them with stones before undermining the gates under a testudo. Caesar sent Numidian, Cretan and Balearic missile troops at night and the siege was lifted.

battle.significance: Prelude to the standoff on the Axona.

events.title: Surrender of the Suessiones and Bellovaci
events.summary: After the Belgic coalition dispersed, Caesar marched on Noviodunum of the Suessiones, whose inhabitants surrendered in terror at the sight of his siege towers and vineae; the Bellovaci gave up at Bratuspantium at the intercession of Diviciacus, and the Ambiani followed.

battle.significance: Broke the southern Belgae before the campaign against the Nervii.

events.title: Publius Crassus receives the submission of Armorica
events.summary: With a single legion Publius Crassus, Caesar's young legate and son of the triumvir, received the submission of the Veneti, Venelli, Osismi, Coriosolites, Esuvii, Aulerci and Redones. Caesar announced all Gaul pacified; the Veneti revolted the following winter by seizing Crassus' requisitioning officers.

events.title: Cicero recovers his house: De domo sua
events.summary: Returning from exile on 4 September 57, Cicero argued before the pontifical college on 29 September that Clodius' consecration of his house site was invalid because Clodius' adoption and tribunate were unlawful. The pontiffs found for him and the Senate voted compensation, but Clodius' gangs attacked the builders.

events.title: The Sibylline oracle on the king of Egypt
events.summary: In January 56 the tribune Gaius Cato produced a Sibylline oracle, leaked from the quindecimviri, forbidding Rome to restore the king of Egypt 'with a multitude'. It blocked the commission to Publius Lentulus Spinther and Pompey alike, until Gabinius acted without authority in 55.

events.title: De provinciis consularibus: Cicero's palinode
events.summary: After the meeting at Luca, Cicero spoke in the Senate for keeping Caesar in Gaul and for recalling his own enemies Piso from Macedonia and Gabinius from Syria. He privately called the speech his palinode, his recantation, and stopped resisting the dynasts.

events.title: Publius Crassus conquers Aquitania
events.summary: With twelve cohorts and cavalry, Publius Crassus defeated the Sotiates, besieging their town against mining countermines (the Aquitani were skilled copper miners), and accepted the surrender of Adiatuanus and his 600 devoted followers (soldurii). He then stormed the camp of an Aquitanian and Cantabrian army advised by veterans of Sertorius.

battle.significance: Brought south-western Gaul under Roman control.

events.title: Sabinus defeats Viridovix
events.summary: Quintus Titurius Sabinus, with three legions among the Venelli of the Cotentin, feigned fear and had a Gallic auxiliary 'desert' to report him ready to flee; the Gauls under Viridovix charged uphill at his camp, exhausted, and were routed.

battle.significance: Secured Normandy while Caesar fought the Veneti.

events.title: Caesar's late campaign against the Morini and Menapii
events.summary: At the end of 56 Caesar marched against the Morini and Menapii on the Channel coast, who withdrew into forests and marshes; he began cutting down woods to reach them but autumn rains forced him into winter quarters.

events.title: Pro Sestio: 'cum dignitate otium'
events.summary: Defending the tribune Publius Sestius on a charge of violence brought by Clodian supporters, Cicero delivered a manifesto for a broad 'party of the best' (optimates), all honest and propertied citizens united for peace with dignity. Sestius was acquitted unanimously.

events.title: Pro Caelio
events.summary: Marcus Caelius Rufus, Cicero's former pupil, was prosecuted for violence, including the murder of the Alexandrian envoy Dio and an attempt to poison Clodia Metelli, during the Megalensian games. Cicero turned the case into a demolition of Clodia, 'the Medea of the Palatine', and won an acquittal.
events.detail: The speech is one of the great comic performances of Latin oratory, with Cicero impersonating Clodia's stern ancestor Appius Claudius Caecus and then her playboy brother. If Clodia is Catullus' Lesbia, as Apuleius says, Caelius may be the Rufus of the poems who stole her from the poet.
events.debate: Identification of Clodia with Lesbia rests on Apuleius, Apology 10, and is accepted by most but not all scholars.

events.title: The elephants at Pompey's games
events.summary: At the games for the dedication of his theatre Pompey staged five days of beast hunts with some 500 lions, 410 leopards and the first rhinoceros and lynx seen at Rome, and on the last day twenty elephants fought Gaetulian hunters. When the wounded elephants seemed to plead for mercy the crowd turned against Pompey and cursed him.

events.title: Lex Licinia de sodaliciis
events.summary: Crassus, as consul, carried a law against the use of organised clubs (sodalicia) to canvass and bribe tribes, with an unusual procedure in which the prosecutor named four tribes and the defendant rejected one to form the jury. Cicero's Pro Plancio (54) was delivered under it.

events.title: Lucretius' De rerum natura
events.summary: Titus Lucretius Carus' didactic poem in six books expounds Epicurean physics in Latin hexameters: atoms and void, the mortality of the soul, the origins of the world, civilisation, disease. Cicero wrote to his brother in February 54 that it had 'many flashes of genius, yet much art'. Jerome's later story that a love-potion drove Lucretius mad is now generally rejected.
events.detail: The poem is dedicated to Gaius Memmius, praetor 58, a patron of poets whose career collapsed after the electoral scandal of 54. Lucretius set out to free readers from fear of the gods and of death by showing that everything, including the mind, is made of atoms that dissolve; its plague of Athens finale, based on Thucydides, ends abruptly, perhaps unfinished. A papyrus of Philodemus' library at Herculaneum contains fragments of Lucretius, and the work survived the Middle Ages in two Carolingian manuscripts before Poggio Bracciolini's rediscovery of 1417 made it a founding text of early modern materialism.
events.debate: Dates of Lucretius' life (c. 99-55 or 94-51) rest on Jerome and Donatus and conflict; whether Cicero edited the poem after the poet's death, as Jerome claims, is doubtful.

events.title: Cicero's De oratore
events.summary: Cicero's three-book dialogue on the ideal orator, set in 91 at the villa of Lucius Licinius Crassus in the days before his death, presents Crassus and Marcus Antonius debating whether the orator needs universal learning. Written in the political sidelines after Luca, it is his first great dialogue.

events.title: The tribune Ateius curses Crassus' departure
events.summary: As Crassus left Rome in November 55 for Syria and the war with Parthia, the tribune Gaius Ateius Capito tried to arrest him, then at the city gate lit a brazier and pronounced dire curses invoking strange gods. After Carrhae the censor Appius Claudius expelled Ateius from the Senate for falsifying the auspices.

events.title: Crassus' first campaign in Mesopotamia
events.summary: Crassus crossed the Euphrates at Zeugma in 54, received the submission of Greek cities such as Ichnae, Nicephorium and Carrhae, stormed Zenodotium after it killed a hundred of his soldiers, and was saluted imperator. He then withdrew to winter in Syria, leaving garrisons, which Plutarch and Dio judge a fatal loss of momentum.

events.title: Crassus plunders the Temple at Jerusalem
events.summary: Wintering in Syria, Crassus collected funds for his campaign, including the 2,000 talents in the Temple treasury at Jerusalem that Pompey had left untouched, and a golden beam the priest Eleazar gave him on oath that he would take nothing more. He also stripped the temple of Atargatis at Hierapolis.

events.title: The electoral scandal of 54
events.summary: The consular candidates Gaius Memmius and Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus made a pact with the consuls of 54 promising them, in return for support, either three augurs and two ex-consuls to swear falsely to a lex curiata and a senatus consultum on their provinces, or 400,000 sesterces each. Memmius, encouraged by Pompey, read the contract aloud in the Senate. Interest rates doubled from 4 to 8 per cent a month on the eve of the elections.
events.detail: Cicero's letters describe 10 million sesterces promised to the century that voted first, and electoral bribery so open that money became scarce in the city. The scandal postponed the elections until July 53 and destroyed Memmius' career. It is the clearest single demonstration of how the institutions of the Republic had become commodities, and helped prepare opinion for Pompey's emergency consulship of 52.

events.title: The trials of Gabinius
events.summary: Returning from Syria after restoring Ptolemy XII without authority, Aulus Gabinius was acquitted of treason (maiestas) in October 54 amid suspicion of bribery, but then convicted of extortion, with Cicero, under pressure from Pompey, defending his old enemy. Gabinius went into exile; the 10,000 talents he was said to have received from Ptolemy could not be recovered.

events.title: Pro Rabirio Postumo
events.summary: Cicero defended the banker Gaius Rabirius Postumus, who had lent Ptolemy XII the money for his recognition and restoration and then served as the king's finance minister (dioiketes) in Alexandria, wearing Greek dress, before being imprisoned and fleeing. He was charged with receiving part of Gabinius' bribes.

events.title: The Tiber flood of 54
events.summary: A great flood of the Tiber in autumn 54 inundated low-lying parts of Rome and destroyed houses and goods; popular opinion blamed it on the gods' anger at Gabinius' acquittal, and Cicero quoted Homer on Zeus flooding the land of unjust judges.

events.title: Caesar buys land for a new forum
events.summary: Through his agents Cicero and Oppius, Caesar bought private property north-west of the Forum Romanum for a new forum at a cost of 60 million sesterces, rising to 100 million according to Suetonius. The same year Lucius Aemilius Paullus began rebuilding the Basilica Aemilia with Caesar's money and the Basilica Julia was begun on the site of the Basilica Sempronia.

events.title: Labienus kills Indutiomarus
events.summary: Indutiomarus, leader of the Treveri, gathered the Gauls against Labienus' winter camp among the Remi after Atuatuca; Labienus secretly brought in cavalry, offered a reward for Indutiomarus alone, and his horsemen caught and beheaded him at a river ford.

battle.significance: Calmed the north-east for the winter of 54/53.

events.title: The poems of Catullus
events.summary: Gaius Valerius Catullus of Verona, who died young about 54, left a book of 116 poems: short lyrics in Greek metres, epigrams and longer learned pieces including a miniature epic on Peleus and Thetis. His affair with 'Lesbia', usually identified with Clodia Metelli, and his abuse of Caesar and Mamurra made him the voice of the neoteric poets.
events.detail: Catullus dedicated his book to Cornelius Nepos. Suetonius records that Caesar, having been branded in Catullus' verses, accepted his apology and invited him to dinner the same day. The poems survived the Middle Ages in a single manuscript found at Verona about 1300 and since lost.

events.title: Brutus' LIBERTAS denarius
events.summary: As moneyer about 54, Marcus Junius Brutus struck denarii showing the head of Libertas and, on the reverse, his ancestor Lucius Junius Brutus, the first consul, walking between lictors; another type paired the founder with Servilius Ahala, killer of the would-be tyrant Maelius. The ancestry Brutus advertised was quoted at him by those urging him to kill Caesar.

events.title: No consuls until July: the interregnum of 53
events.summary: Because of bribery scandals, tribunician obstruction and calls for Pompey's dictatorship, no consuls were elected for 53 until July, when Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus and Marcus Valerius Messalla Rufus were finally chosen under a succession of interreges. Violence prevented elections for 52 as well.

events.title: Labienus defeats the Treveri
events.summary: Labienus, facing the Treveri across a river with 25 cohorts, pretended to retreat in panic so that the Gauls crossed to attack on bad ground, then turned and routed them before German reinforcements arrived. Power among the Treveri passed to Caesar's ally Cingetorix.

battle.significance: Secured the Moselle region before Caesar's Rhine crossing.

events.title: Caesar's second Rhine bridge
events.summary: To punish the Suebi for aiding the Treveri, Caesar built a second timber bridge over the Rhine a little upstream of the first, probably near Neuwied or Urmitz. The Suebi withdrew into the forest of Bacenis and Caesar returned after a few days, demolishing the end of the bridge and leaving a tower and garrison.
